items.case: permanent situations or states
examples: She works as a nurse.
She owns a large shop.

items.case: repeated / habitual actions (especially with frequency adverbs: often, usually, etc.)
examples: I usually get up at 7:30 am.

items.case: permanent truths or laws of nature
examples: Money doesn't buy happiness.
Water freezes at 0°C.

items.case: timetables / programmes (future meaning)
examples: The match finishes at 7:45 pm.
The plane leaves at 6:05 am.

items.case: reviews / sports commentaries / dramatic narratives
examples: Angelina Jolie acts brilliantly in this film.

items.case: temporary situations
examples: They're staying at the Park Hotel at present.

items.case: actions happening at or around the moment of speaking
examples: She is looking for a better job.

items.case: repeated actions with always, expressing annoyance or criticism
examples: She's always interrupting me!

items.case: fixed arrangements in the near future
examples: The Browns are visiting us tonight.

items.case: changing or developing situations
examples: His English is getting better.

items.case: recently completed actions
examples: She has tidied her room.
items.hint: She has finished tidying her room. You can see it is tidy now — evidence in the present.

items.case: actions which happened at an unstated time in the past and are connected with the present
examples: He has lost his keys.
items.hint: He is still looking for them.

items.case: personal experiences / change that has happened over a period of time
examples: I've lost weight.

items.case: emphasis on number
examples: She's written three letters since this morning.
She has spoken to two clients since 12 o'clock.

items.case: actions started in the past and continuing up to the present
examples: He's been writing a letter for two hours.
items.hint: He started two hours ago and he's still writing.

items.case: past actions of certain duration having visible results or effects in the present
examples: She's been crying.

items.case: actions expressing anger, irritation, annoyance, explanation or criticism
examples: Who has been using my hairbrush?

items.case: emphasis on duration (usually with for, since or how long)
examples: They have been speaking in his office for the last hour.

blocks.heading: NOTE
items: live, feel and work can be used either in the present perfect or the present perfect continuous with no difference in meaning. I've been living / I've lived in Rome for a year.

items.v: every day / week / month / year, usually, often, always, rarely, never, sometimes, in the morning / evening / afternoon, at night, on Mondays
now, at the moment, at present, nowadays, today, tonight, always, still
just, ever, never, already, yet (negations and questions), always, how long, so far, recently, since (= from a starting point in the past), for (= over a period of time), today, this week / month

items.case: past actions which happened immediately one after the other
examples: She sealed the letter, put a stamp on it and posted it.

items.case: action or event which happened at a stated past time
examples: She called an hour ago.

items.case: action which happened at a definite past time. The action was completed in the past
examples: Shakespeare wrote a lot of plays.
items.hint: Shakespeare is now dead; he won't write again.

items.case: past habit or state
examples: He used to go / went to school on foot.

items.case: two or more simultaneous past actions
examples: While I was sunbathing, Tim was swimming.

items.case: action in progress at a stated time in the past
examples: He was playing tennis at 4:30 pm yesterday.

items.case: past action in progress interrupted by another past action
examples: While I was getting dressed the bell rang.
items.hint: The longer action is in the Past Continuous, the shorter action is in the Past Simple.

items.case: background description to events in a story
examples: She was flying to Paris. The sun was shining...

items.case: past action which occurred before another past action or before a specific time in the past
examples: He had left by the time I got there.

items.case: complete past action which had visible results in the past
examples: She was sad because she had failed the test.

items.case: the Past Perfect is the past equivalent of the Present Perfect
examples: He can't find his watch. He has lost it.
He couldn't find his watch. He had lost it.

items.case: emphasis on the duration of an action which started and finished in the past before another past action or a stated time in the past
examples: She had been working as a clerk for 10 years before she resigned.

items.case: past action of certain duration which had visible results in the past
examples: They were wet because they had been walking in the rain.

items.case: the Past Perfect Continuous is the past equivalent of the Present Perfect Continuous
examples: She is going to the doctor. Her leg has been aching for two days.
She went to the doctor. Her leg had been aching for two days.

items.v: yesterday, last week, etc., (how long) ago, then, just now, when, in 1967
for, since, already, after, just, never, yet, before, by, by the time

items.case: decisions taken at the moment of speaking (on-the-spot decisions)
examples: It's getting dark, I'll turn on the light.

items.case: hopes, fears, threats, offers, promises, warnings, predictions, requests, comments, especially with expect, hope, believe, I'm sure, I'm afraid, probably
examples: I'm afraid I'll be a little late.

items.case: future predictions based on what we think or imagine will happen
examples: They'll probably go shopping on Tuesday.

items.case: facts in the future
examples: He will be ten next year.

items.case: things we are not sure about or haven't decided to do yet
examples: She'll probably pass the test.

items.case: future plans and intentions
examples: Now that they've settled in their new house, they're going to have a party.

items.case: predictions based on what we can see or what we know, especially when there is evidence
examples: Ann is going to have a baby.
Look at the dark clouds in the sky! It's going to rain.

items.case: things we are sure about or we have already decided to do in the near future
examples: Max is going to invite his friends to dinner.
items.hint: He has already decided to do this.

items.case: actions in progress at a stated future time
examples: He'll be sunbathing in Hawaii this time next week.

items.case: actions which are the result of a routine (instead of the Present Continuous)
examples: I'll be seeing John tomorrow.
items.hint: We work in the same office so we'll definitely meet.

items.case: when we ask politely about people's arrangements, to see if they can do something for us or because we want to offer to do something for them
examples: Will you be going to the supermarket? Can you buy me some tea?

items.case: actions which will have finished before a stated future time
examples: She will have come back by the end of July.

items.case: by or not ... until / till are used with the Future Perfect. Until / till are normally used with the Future Perfect only in negative sentences
examples: She will have finished by 8 o'clock.
She won't have finished until 8 o'clock.
items.hint: NOT: She will have finished until 8 o'clock.

blocks.heading: AND TWO PRESENT FORMS WITH FUTURE MEANING

items.v: timetables and programmes. The plane reaches London at 9:45 pm.
fixed arrangements in the near future. Sally is seeing her dentist tomorrow afternoon. (Sally has already made an appointment.)
emphasis on the duration of an action up to a certain time in the future. By the end of this year, Sally will have been working here for two years.
